compositionPlan.coldReadTarget: After a minute a newcomer can say what the page answers: Is this the planning flow Brian wants every project on: facts decide trivial vs emergency vs real work, real work needs an adopted plan that writes its /goal, and the commit hook checks every lane?
sketchInstructions: Put one short title at the top that states what this page answers and for whom.
Everything important is visible at once; no scrolling implied.
One main drawing occupies most of the area; other elements are visibly smaller and lighter.
Use at most three type sizes; headings heavier than body; important boxes larger.
Entry point top-left; the thing to do next bottom-right; if the order differs, number the parts.
Related items touch or nearly touch; unrelated items have clear gaps between them.
Every object of one kind is drawn the same way in every picture of the set.
Left edges of text and boxes line up on a few shared vertical lines.
Reuse one card style, one label style, and one legend position across the set.
Leave generous empty space around the main drawing and between groups.
No decorative borders, shadows, icons, or gridlines that carry no meaning.
Any colour or badge used has its meaning shown right there.
A small status line shows source and date.
Exactly one kind of thing is highlighted; everything else is grey scale.
Draw each part in the form that fits its job: list, table, flow, or map.
Connections are lines or containment, not just items placed near each other.
Every claim attributed to a person points at where they said it; leave a table cell empty rather than fill it.
Only draw a border, number or label where it tells the reader something; never number things that are not a sequence.
Before drawing, ask whether this page would look the same for an unrelated subject; if so, change the defaults.
Give each concept the shape of its behaviour; do not draw equal boxes for things that behave differently.
One large drawing with a few short labels pointing at parts of it; no columns of text.
Only draw a section or tab if the content shown needs it.
A stranger should get the point from the title and the main drawing alone.
Show a handful of objects at readable size, not dozens at tiny size.
Show each answer as a picture first (a path, bars, a strip of days, a map); use a sentence only where nothing visual says it better.
Draw boxes and arrows only where things branch, loop back meaningfully, connect many-to-many, or pass typed data between ports; a straight chain of steps is a numbered list.
No ellipses: boxes and labels grow to fit their whole text; lists of points are bullets.
Sketch both the phone layout and the laptop layout.
Draw a Sources list in the control column under Topics; one source selected, with its links glowing in the diagram and its quote in the details panel.
Annotate the sketch with the three viewports the checks run at.
Write every tour step or callout as one to five short bullet points, never a paragraph.
